mechGEA

Background

mechGEA is a mechanistic genotype–environment association (GEA) pipeline for identifying loci involved in local adaptation, designed to work directly with low-coverage sequencing data.

Why a mechanistic GEA?

Most GEA methods have two limitations:

  1. They ignore uncertainty in genotyping and cannot have missing data. Allele frequencies are estimated from a finite, often incomplete sample of genotypes, and with low-coverage data the genotypes themselves are uncertain. Treating these estimates as known can bias downstream inference. Similarly, they typically also do not allow missing data, requiring imputation or a similar approach prior to use.
  2. They are phenomenological. Regression-based approaches (e.g. GLMs) assume a particular shape for the relationship between environment and allele frequency, but are only loosely connected to evolutionary theory.

mechGEA instead builds the analysis on an explicit model of evolution and incorporates uncertainty into the model directly via data model.

Installation

mechGEA fits models with Stan via cmdstanr and rstan. Installing these dependencies manually can be difficult, in part because they must be installed in a particular order under different C++ compiler versions. The usual installation tools (install.packages or the remotes and pak packages) cannot handle this on their own; installing with these tools alone will only produce a partial-install.

We therefore strongly recommend installing mechGEA into a dedicated conda environment using a two-step process via the function setup_mechGEA_env() included in mechGEA.

mechGEA is currently tested and maintained for Linux only. Support for Windows and macOS is limited.

1. Initial install of mechGEA from GitHub, using remotes or pak:

install.packages("remotes") # skip if already installed!
remotes::install_github("hemstrow/mechGEA")

This will install the package, but the core functions will be turned off unless mechGEA detects a complete install.

2. Build the complete environment with setup_mechGEA_env():

mechGEA::setup_mechGEA_env() # creates a conda environment called "mechGEA"

This builds a self-contained conda environment (using the reticulate package) with everything mechGEA needs: R, C/C++/Fortran compilers, CmdStan, cmdstanr, rstan, sf, terra, all other dependencies, and mechGEA itself. No system libraries or administrator rights are required. - If conda is not found, Miniconda is installed automatically. To use an existing conda installation (other than the default), provide a path to the conda executable: setup_mechGEA_env(conda_path = "/path/to/conda"). - Use name to choose a different environment name. The function stops if an environment with that name already exists. - Setup compiles several packages and can take a long time. At the end, check that the printed CmdStan path points inside the conda environment.

3. Activate the environment in bash to run analyses, then either run an R script or start up an R session:

conda activate mechGEA
Rscript path/to/my_analysis.R

Quick-start Guide

Here, we will walk through a basic analysis of the example data included in this package (example_gl and sample_metadata): 200 individuals sampled across 20 patches, genotyped at 1,500 loci, with five environmental variables. We will look at the input formats, prepare patch metadata, estimate migration among patches, fit the mechanistic GEA model, and summarise and plot the results. We first run the full pipeline with a single call to mechGEA(), then step through each stage individually.

library(mechGEA)
#> Loading required package: data.table
#> Warning: package 'data.table' was built under R version 4.5.3
#> mechGEA version: 0.0.0.9000 loaded.
#> ================================================================================

#> While this version is passing all tests, there may still be bugs present.
#> Please report any issues to the github issues page (https://github.com/hemstrow/mechGEA/issues)!
#> Check out the NEWS page on github for update notes (https://github.com/hemstrow/mechGEA/blob/dev/NEWS.md)
#> ================================================================================

Data import

mechGEA needs four inputs:

Input Description
Phred Phred-scaled genotype likelihoods, one row per locus and one column per individual; genotypes comma separated with missing data marked “.”
patch_info Patch identification for each individual
patches_xy Coordinates of each patch
env Z-scaled (mean 0, sd 1), uncorrelated environmental variables for each patch

For the example data, all four are stored in the example_gl list:

Important: Individuals in sample_metadata must be in the same order as the columns (individuals) of the genotype likelihoods, and all individuals from the same patch must be in consecutive rows. Patches must in patches_xy and env must also be sorted by order-of-appearance in patch_info.

str(example_gl, max.level = 1)
#> List of 4
#>  $ likelihoods: chr [1:1500, 1:200] "46,6,0" "138,18,0" "." "69,9,0" ...
#>   ..- attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2
#>  $ patch_info :'data.frame': 200 obs. of  2 variables:
#>  $ patches_xy :'data.frame': 20 obs. of  3 variables:
#>  $ env        :'data.frame': 20 obs. of  6 variables:

Generating correctly formatted metadata from an sf object.

If your sample metadata is stored per individual in an sf object with one row per individual and environmental values attached, as in the sample_metadata example data, theprepare_metadata() function can be used to convert it into patch_info, patches_xy, and env objects:

head(sample_metadata)
#>      patch  ind_id        env1      env2       env3     env4     env5
#> 1 patch_01 ind_001 -0.03212425 0.2021607 -0.6491746 1.558552 1.141542
#> 2 patch_01 ind_002 -0.03212425 0.2021607 -0.6491746 1.558552 1.141542
#> 3 patch_01 ind_003 -0.03212425 0.2021607 -0.6491746 1.558552 1.141542
#> 4 patch_01 ind_004 -0.03212425 0.2021607 -0.6491746 1.558552 1.141542
#> 5 patch_01 ind_005 -0.03212425 0.2021607 -0.6491746 1.558552 1.141542
#> 6 patch_01 ind_006 -0.03212425 0.2021607 -0.6491746 1.558552 1.141542
#>               geometry
#> 1 -105.65012, 46.04031
#> 2 -105.65012, 46.04031
#> 3 -105.65012, 46.04031
#> 4 -105.65012, 46.04031
#> 5 -105.65012, 46.04031
#> 6 -105.65012, 46.04031
meta <- prepare_metadata(sample_metadata)

It is important to note that the GEA model assumes environmental variables are uncorrelated and Z-scaled. The prune_envs() function can be used to prune highly correlated environmental variables according to a correlation threshold by sequentially removing the variables correlated with the highest number of other variables. prune_envs() also Z-scales data.

# removes one env from any pair with a correlation coefficient above 0.7
# (or below -0.7).
meta$env <- prune_envs(meta$env, r2 = 0.7)

The resulting, correctly formatted data should be essentially identical to that in the example_gl data set, albeit without genotypes.

Patch metadata details:

patch_info is a two-column data.frame with columns ind_id and patch. Its rows must be in the same order as the columns of Phred, and individuals must be sorted in blocks by patch: all individuals from one patch must be in a block (sorted next to each other).

head(example_gl$patch_info)
#>    ind_id    patch
#> 1 ind_001 patch_01
#> 2 ind_002 patch_01
#> 3 ind_003 patch_01
#> 4 ind_004 patch_01
#> 5 ind_005 patch_01
#> 6 ind_006 patch_01

patches_xy gives coordinates for each patch, with columns patch, lat and lon. env has a patch column followed by one column per environmental variable, each Z-scaled (mean = 0, sd = 1). Lat/lon coordinates are recommended to be in “WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)” coordinate reference for automatic plotting, but this is not required. Both must list patches in the same order in which patches first appear in patch_info.

head(example_gl$patches_xy)
#>      patch      lat       lon
#> 1 patch_01 46.04031 -105.6501
#> 2 patch_02 38.38710 -105.3495
#> 3 patch_03 46.88892 -114.1371
#> 4 patch_04 46.46668 -106.7890
#> 5 patch_05 37.82438 -109.3364
#> 6 patch_06 42.14212 -110.9922
head(example_gl$env)
#>      patch        env1       env2        env3         env4        env5
#> 1 patch_01 -0.03212425  0.2021607 -0.64917455  1.558552048  1.14154181
#> 2 patch_02 -1.36106996 -0.3518810  0.03029178  0.191683584  0.99113613
#> 3 patch_03  0.08928409  0.7416528  0.51805408  0.007063579 -0.98067315
#> 4 patch_04  1.33885570 -0.7091368  1.52398967 -0.220972056  1.76498136
#> 5 patch_05  1.95212686 -1.3359885 -1.09200225 -1.390288050 -0.65674777
#> 6 patch_06 -0.14371808  0.4237745  1.40445240  0.577386601  0.08682305

A quick sanity check before running anything:

patch_order <- unique(example_gl$patch_info$patch)
identical(patch_order, example_gl$patches_xy$patch)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(patch_order, example_gl$env$patch)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(colnames(example_gl$likelihoods), example_gl$patch_info$ind_id)
#> [1] TRUE

All three should be TRUE. Note that these checks are also run automatically.

Genotype likelihoods

Rather than called genotypes, mechGEA uses genotype likelihoods, so uncertainty from low read depth is carried through the model. Each cell holds three comma-separated Phred-scaled likelihoods for the three possible genotypes (homozygous reference, heterozygote, homozygous alternate). Phred-scaling follows the equation: with the lowest Phred-scaled genotype (the most likely genotype) assigned a zero and everything else scaled to that value.

dim(example_gl$likelihoods)          # loci x individuals
#> [1] 1500  200
example_gl$likelihoods[1:5, 1:5]
#>            ind_001    ind_002    ind_003    ind_004   ind_005   
#> locus_0001 "46,6,0"   "0,9,69"   "115,15,0" "8,0,77"  "0,9,69"  
#> locus_0002 "138,18,0" "14,0,37"  "14,0,37"  "46,6,0"  "46,6,0"  
#> locus_0003 "."        "161,21,0" "161,21,0" "37,0,14" "31,0,54" 
#> locus_0004 "69,9,0"   "138,18,0" "138,18,0" "2,0,117" "46,6,0"  
#> locus_0005 "54,0,31"  "92,12,0"  "0,18,138" "92,12,0" "184,24,0"

Genotype likelihoods in BEAGLE format (for example, .beagle.gz output from ANGSD) can be converted to this format with beagle2pl(). Each cell holds three Phred-scaled genotype likelihoods (AA, AB, BB), (again, rescaled so the most likely genotype is 0). Correspondingly, a phred-likelihood of 10 means that genotype is 10× less likely than the likelihood with a score of 0. “.” marks missing data.

An example BEAGLE file is included with the package:

bfile <- system.file("extdata", "example.beagle.gz", package = "mechGEA")
Phred <- beagle2pl(bfile)
dim(Phred)
#> [1] 1500  200

beagle2pl() does not keep sample names from the beagle file by default (since many programs, like ANGSD, name individuals “Ind0” through “Ind(n-1)”). The beagle2pl() function allows for sample names to be provided via the ind_names argument.

Note: this assumes sample_metadata is in the same order as the BAM list used to create the BEAGLE file. If it is not, provide ind_names in the BAM list order and use the ind_order argument to resort individuals on read-in. This can also be used to re-sort individuals which are not in blocks by patch.

colnames(Phred) <- sample_metadata$ind_id
Phred[1:5, 1:5]
#>      ind_001    ind_002    ind_003    ind_004   ind_005   
#> [1,] "46,6,0"   "0,9,69"   "115,15,0" "8,0,77"  "0,9,69"  
#> [2,] "138,18,0" "14,0,37"  "14,0,37"  "46,6,0"  "46,6,0"  
#> [3,] "."        "161,21,0" "161,21,0" "37,0,14" "31,0,54" 
#> [4,] "69,9,0"   "138,18,0" "138,18,0" "2,0,117" "46,6,0"  
#> [5,] "54,0,31"  "92,12,0"  "0,18,138" "92,12,0" "184,24,0"

Running the full pipeline

mechGEA() runs every step of the analysis in one call:

  1. Data preparation: validates the inputs, converts Phred scores to log-likelihoods, and builds the data for both models.
  2. Migration estimation: fits the Bayesian migration model on a random subset of loci.
  3. GEA model fitting: fits the mechanistic GEA model to all loci, accounting for the estimated migration.
  4. Summaries and plots: identifies adaptive (locus, environment) pairs and plots the results.
  5. Effective sample size: estimates effective sample sizes for each locus/ environmental variable pair.

Results are returned as a list and also written to files/ and plot/ in the current working directory, so run it in a dedicated folder.

The settings below are deliberately small so that the example finishes quickly (about an hour on a 22-core server). They are not suitable for real analyses; use the defaults, or larger values, for those.


res <- mechGEA(Phred      = example_gl$likelihoods,
               patch_info = example_gl$patch_info,
               patches_xy = example_gl$patches_xy,
               env        = example_gl$env,
               migration_loci    = 1000,   # loci used to estimate migration
               N_sim_mig         = 20,
               chains_mig        = 2,
               iter_warmup_mig   = 200,
               iter_sampling_mig = 200,
               iter_warmup_gea   = 100,
               iter_sampling_gea = 100,
               par = 12)                   # cores to use
str(res, max.level = 1)

Env/locus pair -log(e) p-values are located in res$SNP_pvalues. res also contains a suite of plots and other outputs. See the vignette for details.

Large datasets

Whole-genome data sets are usually too large to fit in a single model run. The recommended approach is to split the data into chunks of loci and run each chunk separately, ideally in parallel on a computing cluster.

mechGEA has a few utilities to help with this:

  1. get_chunks() splits a “.beagle” or “.beagle.gz” file into chunks containing n loci.
  2. example_slurm_job generates directories, data and metadata files, and a ready-to-run job script for SLURM clusters (which can be modified for other job-management engines). This script will run mechGEA on each BEAGLE chunk.

Splitting data into chunks

get_chunks() splits a BEAGLE file into smaller BEAGLE files of loci_per_chunk loci each, reading the input in pieces so that the full file never has to be loaded into memory. e.g recommended 50k SNPs per chunk at max for whole genome dataset

bfile  <- system.file("extdata", "example.beagle.gz", package = "mechGEA")
chunks <- get_chunks(bfile, 
                     loci_per_chunk = 500, # loci per chunk, use 50-100k for WGS
                     outdir = ".") # save files to pwd. Default uses beagle dir.
chunks
#> [1] "chunk_0.beagle.gz" "chunk_1.beagle.gz" "chunk_2.beagle.gz"

Running on a SLURM cluster

example_slurm_job() generates a SLURM array job that runs mechGEA() on each BEAGLE file as a separate task:

sh <- example_slurm_job(beagle_files    = chunks,
                        sample_metadata = sample_metadata,
                        output_dir      = "results",
                        conda_env       = "mechGEA")
sh

example_slurm_job() takes all of the arguments that mechGEA uses, as well as resource and env pruning arguments.

This writes the following files to ./control/ (change this with control_file_prefix):

File Purpose
example_slurm_array_job.sh SLURM array script, one task per BEAGLE file
example_array_rscript.R R script run by each task
beaglelist.txt list of BEAGLE files
sample_metadata.RDS prepared metadata (patch_info, patches_xy, env)
parmfile.RDS additional arguments passed to mechGEA()

Each task converts its BEAGLE file with beagle2pl(), runs mechGEA() in its own sub-directory of output_dir (partition_<task>_<chunk name>), and writes its results there. The final outputs (e.g. the results of res <- mechGEA(...)) will be saved as final_results.RDS.

To run, edit the example_slurm_array_job.sh for your specific needs and execute.

sbatch example_slurm_array_job.sh
